text:
Jada Williams: Dropping ADR draft for review: ADR-017 Config versioning storage + rollback semantics. Main open question: rollback as “whole-config to prior version” vs “patch rollback (select fields)”.
Link: https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/ARCH/ADR-017-config-versioning-storage-and-rollback-semantics (draft)

Benji Okafor: thx. I skimmed. IMO whole-config rollback is the only thing we can ship safely in v1. Patch rollback quickly turns into “diff language” + conflicts w/ schema changes.

Dylan Brooks: +1 to whole-config for initial. Console UX also gets gnarly if we support partial rollback: people will expect field-level checkboxes, and then we need to explain interactions (batching changes but not caching, etc). That’s a lot.

Sean Gallagher: from on-call POV: simple is good. During incident you want “go back to last known good” not “pick 3 toggles and pray”.
(reactions: :thumbsup: x3)

Mateo Alvarez: runtime angle: patch rollback is not always composable. Example: quantization profile swap + batch scheduler settings.
If you rollback only quant profile but keep new batch settings, we could end up in a state we never validated together. Whole-config gets us back to a tested combo.

Chloe Martin: there’s also concurrency semantics. We’re designing apply/rollback to be idempotent + atomic per scope. A partial rollback means we’re doing “merge” at the control plane, which makes it harder to reason about what exactly was applied.

Marcus Lin: security/compliance: immutable history is easiest when each version is an immutable blob w/ metadata. Patch rollback means “who decided which fields” and “what’s the resulting config” becomes less direct to audit.

Fiona McCarthy: +1. auditors ask “what was the exact config state at time X” and “what was restored at time Y”. Whole-version rollback answers cleanly.

Allison Grant: quick Q: do we lose important use cases if we *don’t* do patch rollback? e.g., one bad field but other fields good.

Sean Gallagher: even if it’s one bad knob, the safer operational practice is: rollback whole config to stabilize, then re-apply with a new version (safe-apply wizard) after validating. That’s still quick.

Jada Williams: ok makes sense. I want to make sure ADR calls out: “whole-config rollback” doesn’t mean “blind revert.” We still do preflight and canary gates (phase 2), right?

Benji Okafor: yep. rollback flow can still be gated by RBAC + justification + we run the same propagation pipeline. But semantics are “set active_version_id = X” and propagate.

Mateo Alvarez: One nuance: runtime has some non-config state. KV cache and warmup behavior.
Even with a full rollback, we may need explicit cache invalidation for certain fields. Otherwise you “rollback” but still see weird latency until caches expire.
We should document which config fields require a cache flush / engine restart / warmup.

Dylan Brooks: yeah this needs to be explicit in ADR + runbook copy. Also in Console: “Rollback will invalidate caches in affected clusters” (or “may trigger warmup”).

Chloe Martin: +1. Control plane can include a “side effects” section in diff preview. At minimum warnings.

Allison Grant: can we list the classes of edge cases? would help for observability too.

Mateo Alvarez: off top of head:
- switching quantization profile (fp16 <-> int8/int4) can change kernel set; rollback may require model reload
- toggling continuous batching params impacts scheduler queues; partial propagation can temporarily split
- prefix/KV cache: if cache key includes quant profile or some batching params, safe; if not, must invalidate
- speculative decoding toggles (if/when) affect tokenization/latency behavior; rollback needs warmup

Sean Gallagher: also: split brain risk. If rollback is triggered while apply is mid-flight, what wins? ADR needs a clear priority rule.

Benji Okafor: ADR currently says “single writer per scope” using lease/lock (control plane + runtime apply locks). If rollback requested while apply in progress, rollback should:
1) acquire lease (or fail fast w/ “apply in progress”)
2) if acquired, create rollback operation w/ new op_id and supersede prior op
But we need to decide “supersede” vs “reject”.

Jada Williams: I lean reject by default unless operator uses an override flag? but during incident you want rollback to win.

Sean Gallagher: rollback should win. If I’m on-call and I click rollback, I don’t want “sorry, someone’s canary is running”.

Fiona McCarthy: from audit standpoint, either is fine as long as we log both attempts + resulting state. But I agree w/ Sean: prioritize rollback.

Marcus Lin: if rollback supersedes, we need to capture provenance: “Rollback op aborted prior apply op <op_id>”. That’s important for change reviews.

Chloe Martin: implementation-wise: easiest is “rollback wins but requires higher permission” (or same permission + reason). We already plan RBAC separation apply vs rollback.

Dylan Brooks: +1. Console can show “This will cancel any in-progress apply for scope X”.

Allison Grant: and metrics: we should emit event when apply aborted by rollback, so dashboards don’t show “random failures”.

Jada Williams: ok, summary of direction I’m hearing:
- ADR decision: Whole-config rollback to immutable prior version (no patch rollback in v1)
- Rollback should supersede/cancel in-flight apply for same scope (with audit trail)
- ADR must explicitly call out runtime side effects and edge cases (cache invalidation, warmup, quant profile swaps, batching queue behavior)

Benji Okafor: yep. I’ll update ADR text accordingly. Can we also add a “documented exceptions” section?
E.g., some fields might be auto-populated at apply time (computed defaults) and won’t exactly match old version on rollback unless we store canonical form.

Ethan Park: +1 on canonicalization. We should store canonical config blob as applied (post-defaulting) so rollback is exact.
If we *must* recompute defaults, we should record the resolver version / schema version.

Chloe Martin: we already have schema_version field in the store design; can add resolver_version too.

Mateo Alvarez: re: edge cases doc — we should track them somewhere besides the ADR. ADR should link to a living “known issues / mitigations” page (runtime-owned) and the SRE runbook.

Sean Gallagher: +1. We’ll need runbook callouts: “rollback succeeded but p95 still high? check warmup panels; cache flush status; model reload time”.

Jada Williams: action items:
- Benji: update ADR w/ decision + rollback supersedes apply semantics + canonicalization notes
- Mateo: start edge cases section / link to runtime known-issues page (KV cache, batching, quant swaps, warmup)
- Sean/Allison: list minimal observability signals we must have to safely GA (rollback op status, cache flush indicator, abort reason)

Dylan Brooks: cool. Once ADR updated I’ll pull it into the PRD “non-goals” + Console copy. Also will add “partial rollback not supported (v1)” to the UI help text so we don’t create expectations.
(reactions: :thumbsup: x4)

Fiona McCarthy: pls make sure ADR explicitly states retention/immutability assumptions (enterprise). Security review will look for “cannot mutate prior versions” and “audit record for every rollback attempt”.

Benji Okafor: ack. Will add.

Jada Williams: thanks all. I’ll mark this thread as resolved once Benji pushes the ADR update + links edge cases page.
